label: Strategies
labelTooltip: Sensory strategies recommended for this child's sensory profile

children.text: Provide regular, scheduled sensory breaks throughout the day to help the CYP manage heightened internal signals
Use visual supports such as body maps or emotion scales to help the CYP identify and label internal body signals
Offer a calm, low-stimulation area where the CYP can go when feeling overwhelmed by internal sensations
Teach and practise regulation strategies such as box breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, or grounding techniques
Provide predictable routines and visual schedules around eating, drinking, and toileting to reduce anxiety about internal sensations
Use social stories to help the CYP understand and manage their responses to internal signals such as hunger, pain, or temperature changes
Work with the CYP to create a personalised regulation toolkit that includes preferred calming strategies
Allow flexible access to water, snacks, and toilet facilities to reduce distress from heightened awareness of internal needs
Implement scheduled prompts for toileting, eating, and drinking rather than relying on the CYP to recognise their own needs
Use visual timetables or timers as prompts for regular hydration and meal breaks
Teach the CYP to use a body check-in routine at regular intervals to notice internal sensations
Use the Zones of Regulation or similar programme to develop emotional awareness and link feelings to body signals
Use heart rate activities such as feeling a pulse after exercise to help the CYP notice and compare body sensations
Provide explicit teaching about what different internal signals feel like using concrete examples and visuals
Incorporate movement breaks such as jumping, yoga, or running on the spot to amplify internal body sensations
Use body mapping activities and diagrams to help the CYP mark where sensations occur and describe them
Teach emotion-sensation pairing to link feelings to body cues, e.g. 'tight chest = anxious', using visual supports and concrete language
Provide support to link internal body signals to actions, e.g. 'When your tummy growls, that means you are hungry'
Use resources from Kelly Mahler's interoception curriculum to develop body-signal awareness
Use journaling or visual logs to record sensations and possible triggers, helping the CYP build patterns over time
Allow for flexible seating and positioning options so the CYP can find comfortable positions
Use non-slip mats for stability, ensure tables and chairs are at the correct height, and provide seating aids such as a Movin'Sit cushion
Offer adapted tools for fine motor tasks such as thicker pencils or pencil grips to reduce proprioceptive demand
Allow the CYP to stand or move during tasks if sitting is uncomfortable
Use weighted lap pads or weighted teddies to provide calming proprioceptive input (weighted vests only if approved by an OT)
Provide regular heavy work activities such as carrying books, pushing, pulling, or wall press-ups
Provide jumping, climbing, and playground equipment activities such as trampolines, monkey bars, and climbing frames
Incorporate resistive activities such as wall pushes, tug of war, or working with TheraBands into movement breaks
Use threading, kneading dough, and other fine motor resistive activities to build proprioceptive awareness
Use a wobble cushion, therapy ball, or move-n-sit cushion for seating to increase proprioceptive feedback
Encourage the CYP to help with physical classroom tasks such as stacking chairs or moving equipment
Provide fidget tools such as stress balls, tangles, or pencil toppers for the CYP to use during lessons
Allow access to resistance bands on chair legs, TheraBands, or textured items for proprioceptive feedback
Use a movement cushion, T-stool, or therapy ball for proprioceptive feedback during seated tasks
Schedule structured movement breaks such as Brain Gym to reset body awareness
Provide threading activities and fine motor tasks for proprioceptive awareness
Use visual cues such as coloured tape for body positioning and personal space boundaries
Offer a Swiss or gym ball for leaning and additional sensory feedback during focus tasks
Ensure access to handrails on stairs and allow stair use during quieter times to reduce anxiety
Provide advance warning before any activities involving movement, changes of direction, or heights
Offer grounding opportunities such as sitting on the floor or holding onto something stable
Avoid fast start/stop movements; use slow, rhythmic rocking to help soothe and calm the CYP
Enlist a buddy for support during movement activities to increase confidence and sense of safety
Break down movement activities into small steps with visual cues and offer predictable routines for transitions
Provide stability aids such as a stable chair (not a swivel chair) and ensure feet can touch the floor
Provide regular opportunities for controlled movement activities such as rocking, swinging, or bouncing
Offer activities that involve crossing the midline, such as lazy eights, to build vestibular processing
Build movement breaks into the daily routine to meet the CYP's need for vestibular stimulation
Provide access to climbing frames, monkey bars, trampolines, and balance activities
Allow the CYP to run errands or carry out jobs that involve walking around the school
Allow the CYP to stand or move while working if remaining still is difficult
Schedule regular movement breaks with spinning, swinging, or bouncing activities
Provide gentle rocking or swinging options using wobble chairs, Hokki stools, or ball chairs
Include rhythmic and musical games such as rowing games and partner activities like wheelbarrows
Offer yoga for children such as Cosmic Yoga as a structured way to meet vestibular needs
Incorporate rhythmic movement such as marching, skipping, or dancing into transitions
Allow the CYP to use alternative positions such as kneeling or lying on their belly to read or work
Use wobble chairs or one-legged stools to allow safe movement while seated
Seat the CYP near the back or side of the class so they can see others approaching, and place at the front or back of lines
Forewarn before any physical contact — say the CYP's name first and always approach from the front
Provide a defined sitting area such as a carpet tile and ensure others are not sitting too close
Do not force messy play; offer alternatives such as paintbrushes or allow gloves for aversive textures
Provide a towel on the chair or carpet if the texture is distracting or uncomfortable
Arrange the classroom to minimise accidental jostling and allow early entry to busy spaces such as the dinner hall
Remember that hugs may be painful rather than comforting — approach gently and respect the CYP's boundaries
Provide opportunities for messy play, water play, and tactile exploration
Gradually introduce different textures using tools first, such as spoons or glove fingers, before progressing to direct touch
Use play dough, Theraputty, and modelling activities to build tactile tolerance and fine motor skills
Create obstacle courses with different textures such as towels, carpet, and bubble wrap
Include cutting, sticking, threading, and collage activities to provide varied tactile experiences
Provide a box of tactile items (koosh balls, putty, textured fabrics) for the CYP to access during lessons
Allow tactile self-regulation such as stroking a preferred fabric, tapping fingers, or rubbing a worry stone
Offer fidget tools that provide tactile input such as tangles, putty, or textured fidgets
Provide opportunities for finger painting, colouring, or drawing as structured tactile outlets
Encourage clapping hands, giving high fives, or holding a stuffed animal as safe ways to meet tactile needs
Use texture bins with a variety of preferred materials for the CYP to explore during sensory breaks
Reduce visual clutter in the classroom — use neutral colours, minimal displays, and organised storage
Seat the CYP away from windows and visual distractions; allow the use of a cap or sunglasses, at least outdoors
Use pastel or cream-coloured paper instead of white to reduce glare
Limit visual material on walls and ceilings; store resources out of sight or cover with plain fabric
Reduce fluorescent lighting where possible and consider deep-coloured bulbs to minimise glare
Provide a screened-off workstation with high sides and blank walls if the classroom is visually busy
Offer coloured acetate strips or a reading window to reduce visual overload when reading
Avoid demanding eye contact; allow alternative gaze strategies such as looking near the eyes or hairline
Use visual timetables, personalised schedules, and visual cues such as traffic lights to support regulation
Colour-code workbooks, timetables, and classroom doors to support orientation and organisation
Use sign language or Makaton alongside spoken instructions to reinforce understanding
Use real objects and concrete materials to explain abstract ideas
Use exaggerated facial expressions and clear body language to support communication
Define the layout of the room with physical boundaries and clear spatial organisation
Provide sorting, counting, and building activities such as Lego or stacking to develop visual engagement
Allow small visual toys in a sensory box for scheduled sensory breaks
Provide glitter calm-down jars, bubbles, or light-up toys for visual stimulation
Encourage the CYP to look at clouds, stars, or sky as a calming visual strategy
Offer visual games such as throwing and catching, stacking, or sorting activities
Provide a visual sensory box with items such as kaleidoscopes, fidget spinners, or reflective materials
Teach the CYP to look away from stimuli when feeling dysregulated as a self-regulation strategy
Provide ear defenders or noise-cancelling headphones for use in noisy environments
Pre-warn the CYP before any expected loud noises such as fire alarm tests, bells, or assemblies
Allow the CYP to leave noisy environments or arrive/leave slightly early to avoid busy transition times
Shut doors and windows to reduce external noise and seat the CYP away from background noise sources such as fans or doorways
Use soft furnishings, carpeting, and felt pads on furniture to minimise extraneous noise in the classroom
Provide a quiet, low-stimulation space for the CYP to retreat to when overwhelmed
Offer a ballpoint pen if the sound of pencil on paper is uncomfortable, and use visual cues alongside verbal communication
Allow the CYP to listen to music through headphones, including various genres and natural sound recordings
Provide opportunities to play with sound-making items such as whistles, kazoos, or drums in outdoor settings
Use white, pink, or brown noise to support engagement and regulation during focused tasks
Create listening games and sound maps — sit quietly outdoors and identify sounds and their direction
Let the CYP control volume levels and explore the difference between soft and loud sounds
Provide headphones with music during independent work if this supports focus
Offer access to musical instruments or sound-making toys at appropriate times
If the CYP needs to hum to concentrate, teach them to do so quietly and position them where it is less distracting
Incorporate rhythm and music into learning activities
Provide a vibrating toy or cushion to meet the CYP's need for auditory and tactile feedback
Use natural sound recordings and listening games to channel auditory seeking productively
Allow the CYP to explore controlling volume levels to satisfy their interest in sound
Do not remove preferred foods or force the CYP to try new foods; avoid hiding or altering preferred items
Reduce background noise during mealtimes and provide calming objects or preferred smells to ease anxiety
Offer alternatives for mixed textures and use visual timetables to prepare the CYP for mealtimes
Communicate with staff about the CYP's sensitivities and avoid placing pressure on them around food
Consider seating comfort at mealtimes and allow distractions such as a preferred toy to reduce stress
Play games around the table to reduce anxiety and make mealtimes a more positive experience
Provide continued exposure to food-related activities separate from mealtimes to build familiarity
Use graded desensitisation steps: place food on the table, then the plate, then encourage touching, licking, and eventually tasting
Use food charts and food books with pictures of liked and disliked foods, updating as the CYP tries new items
Encourage the CYP to handle and prepare food, look through recipe books, and choose appealing options
Offer strong-flavoured foods such as citrus or mint in a controlled way at planned times
Provide alternative strong smells during mealtimes, such as lavender, mint, or citrus
Encourage food preparation and cooking activities for tactile and olfactory input
Use playful exploration such as guessing flavours or food-related games to channel seeking
Allow sensory items or a preferred toy at the table to meet sensory needs while eating
Avoid strong-scented products such as perfumes, air fresheners, and cleaning products; use unscented materials where possible
Seat the CYP away from potential odour sources such as kitchens, toilets, or bins
Allow the CYP to use a preferred scent on a handkerchief or wristband to mask unpleasant smells
If strong smells cannot be avoided, close doors, position the CYP near an open window, or use a small fan
Use social stories where avoidance behaviours are affecting safety or participation, e.g. refusing to enter the hall due to food smells
Provide opportunities to experience different smells using graded exposure — start with a sniff from a distance and build tolerance gradually
Fill containers with various smelling items and play guessing, matching, and sorting games to develop olfactory awareness
Use structured smell identification activities that link smells to contexts, e.g. 'kitchen = vanilla', 'playground = pine'
Use social stories to build recognition of helpful versus unhelpful responses to smells
Play 'same and different' games with a range of scents to develop olfactory discrimination
Provide safe, acceptable items to smell such as scented markers or cotton pads with a drop of essential oil
Use strong-smelling products to redirect the CYP from inappropriate stimuli to preferred safe smells
Use social stories where seeking behaviours are inappropriate, pairing clear rules with acceptable alternatives
Provide smell jars, matching games, and controlled olfactory exploration activities with clear hygiene routines
